en: Majjhima Nikāya 6: The Discourse on What Might Be Desired (Ākaṅkheyyasutta).
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Bhikkhus, dwell possessed of virtue, possessed of the Pātimokkha; dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing fear in even the slightest faults; undertake and train yourselves in the rules of training.”
“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I be dear and agreeable to my fellow celibates,
respected and esteemed,’ he should fulfill the precepts, be devoted to internal tranquility of mind,
not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty huts.”
“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I be one who obtains robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,’ he should be one who fulfills the precepts,
is devoted to internal mental tranquility, does not neglect jhāna, is possessed of insight,
and frequents empty dwellings.”
“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May the services of those for whom I enjoy robes, almsfood, lodgings,
and medicinal requisites for the sick be of great fruit and great benefit,’ he should be one who fulfills his moral discipline,
is devoted to internal mental tranquility, does not neglect meditative absorption, is endowed with insight, and frequents empty dwellings.”
“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May whatever kinsmen and blood relatives of mine have passed away and died, who remember me with a confident heart,
find that for them this shall be of great fruit and great benefit,’ he should be one who fulfills his moral discipline,
is devoted to internal tranquility of mind, does not neglect jhāna, is possessed of insight, and frequents empty huts.”
“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I be one who overcomes both the unlovely and the lovely; may the unlovely not overcome me;
may I dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen states of the unlovely,’ then he should be one who fulfills the precepts...
[and so on] ...one who frequents empty huts.”
“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I be a conqueror of fear and dread, and may fear and dread not overcome me;
may I dwell having repeatedly overcome whatever fear and dread has arisen,’ then he should be one who fulfills the precepts...
[as before] ...and a frequenter of empty huts.”

“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I be one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts... [and so on] ...let him be a frequenter of empty huts.

If a monk should wish: ‘May I, by realizing them with my own body, dwell in those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending form,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts... [and so on] ...let him be a frequenter of empty huts.”

“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I, through the complete destruction of the three fetters, become a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as my final goal,’ he should be one who fulfills his duties regarding the virtues... [and so on] ...one who frequents empty dwellings.

Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I, through the complete destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hate, and delusion, become a once-returner, returning only once more to this world to make an end of suffering,’ he should be one who fulfills his duties regarding the virtues...”
One who fulfills [the precepts]... [and so on] ... one who cultivates empty dwellings.

Monks, if a monk should wish: "Through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, may I be of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world," then he should be one who fulfills the precepts.
... [and so on] ... one who frequents empty dwellings.
Monks, if a monk should wish: "May I exercise the various kinds of psychic power:
being one, may I become many; being many, may I become one; may I appear and disappear; may I pass through a wall..."
I could walk across a rampart or over a mountain without being obstructed, just as if through space; I could dive in and out of the earth as if it were water;
I could walk on water without breaking the surface, as if on land;
I could travel cross-legged through the air, like a winged bird; and I could touch these very sun and moon, so powerful and majestic...
‘I would touch and stroke with my hand one so endowed with such great power;
I would even exercise mastery over the body as far as the Brahma-world,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts... [and] one who frequents empty dwellings.
If, monks, a monk should desire: ‘With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans...’
‘May I hear both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near’—then he should be one who fulfills the precepts...
[and so on]... one who frequents empty huts.

Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I, by encompassing with my own mind the minds of other beings and other persons, understand them,’ [he should be one who fulfills the precepts... [and so on]... one who frequents empty huts.
One should understand a mind with lust as "a mind with lust," and a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust";
one should understand a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred."
One should know a mind free from hatred as a mind free from hatred;
one should know a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion,
and one should know a mind free from delusion as a mind free from delusion.
One should know a contracted mind as "a contracted mind," one should know a distracted mind as "a distracted mind," and one should know an exalted mind as "an exalted mind."
One should know an unexalted mind as "an unexalted mind";
one should know an surpassed mind as "a surpassed mind," and one should know an unsurpassed mind as "an unsurpassed mind."
One should know a concentrated mind as "a concentrated mind," one should know an unconcentrated mind as "an unconcentrated mind," and one should know a liberated mind as "a liberated mind."
‘May I understand an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind,’ then, monks, he should be one who fulfills his duties regarding the virtues... [as before] ...and one who frequents empty dwellings.
If a monk should wish: ‘May I recollect my manifold past abodes, that is to say, one [birth]...’
One birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births;
many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion: "In such a place I was..."
"Such was my name, such my clan, such my appearance, such my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span;
passing away from there, I arose elsewhere. There too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a life span;
passing away from there, I reappeared here. Thus, with its aspects and particulars, he recollects his manifold past lives.
‘May I recollect my past lives,’ he should be one who fulfills his moral discipline... [and so on] ...one who cultivates empty dwellings.
Monks, if a monk should desire: ‘With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, [may I see beings passing away and being reborn...]’;
May I see beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and may I understand how beings fare according to their kamma:
"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, and possessed of misconduct in mind; they were revilers of the noble ones and held wrong views."
Those who undertook actions based on wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell;
whereas these worthy beings, endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind,
not reviling the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view—
‘With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, may I see beings passing away and being reborn— inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly,
fortunate and unfortunate— and may I understand how beings fare according to their kamma.’”

If, monks, a bhikkhu should wish: “May I, through the destruction of the taints, realize for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, may I dwell therein,” he should be one who fulfills virtuous behavior, who is devoted to internal tranquility of mind, who does not neglect meditation, who is possessed of insight, and who frequents empty huts. If, monks, a bhikkhu should wish:

“May I, through the destruction of the taints, realize for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, may I dwell therein,” he should be one who fulfills virtuous behavior, who is devoted to internal tranquility of mind, who does not neglect meditation, who is possessed of insight, and who frequents empty huts.
“‘Dwell, bhikkhus, perfected in virtue, perfected in the Pātimokkha;
dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults;
train yourselves by undertaking the rules of training’—it was with reference to this that it was said.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The sixth discourse, the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, is concluded.
